title: Organisation
text:
Assessment
The course is worth 5 credits: 100 points in total, 30 from the semester and 70 from the final oral exam. The binding version is the course statement.

Semester — 30 points, at least 15 for the credit
Six graded items, 5 points each. Dates are announced in the e-learning at the start of the semester.








Item
Points
What it covers




Theoretical test 1
5
multiple choice; lectures and labs up to that point


Theoretical test 2
5

Theoretical test 3
5

Practical test — computing
5
by hand: metrics from a confusion matrix, a distance and a k-NN decision, one forward-selection step, a closed-form fit


Practical test — red flags
5
find what is wrong in a given pipeline or agent-written code: leakage, scaling before the split, test set used for model selection, wrong metric


Project
5
ranking of your model on a hidden test set among the other students; one agreed metric



Theoretical tests are taken in the e-learning: 5 questions, 1 point each, one question per page without going back, 8 minutes, no materials. An answer that mixes correct and incorrect options gets zero points; a partially correct selection gets a proportional part of the point. You may ask for a translation or explanation of a question during the test. Retakes are not possible.


Credit requirements

attendance in the computer labs (see Attendance),
at least 15 points from the semester,
coming to the labs with knowledge of the topics already covered in the lectures.



Final exam — 70 points, at least 35 to pass
Oral exam of 20–30 minutes with two examiners. The topics are split into two areas; you draw one question from each area and each examiner grades one of them. The final score is the average of the two, but a substantial lack of knowledge in either area means zero points for the whole exam. You do not have to memorise equations, but you must be able to explain and interpret every equation on the slides. The exam can be taken in Czech or English. Erasmus students who cannot register for a full date should e-mail the guarantor.
The list of topics from the last exam is on the materials page; the 2026/27 list is published before the exam period.

title: Organisation
text:
Attendance

Computer labs are compulsory. At most two excused absences are allowed for the semester.
A missed lab cannot normally be made up at another time. Work through the notebook on your own; the tests assume the material of every lab.
Prolonged absence for serious reasons is dealt with individually: contact the lab teacher or the guarantor as soon as you know about it and a form of compensation will be agreed.

title: Organisation
text:
Rules for using AI

Labs 1–4: switch the AI assistance in Colab off (Settings → AI assistance). You write the code yourself, because the point of these labs is to understand what the algorithm does — including when the code is later written by an agent.
Labs 5–12: a coding agent is part of the work. The faculty provides access, so no subscription of your own is needed; the setup is done in lab 5. Git is mandatory from lab 5 on.
Tests: no AI tools and no materials during the theoretical tests. The practical tests are about understanding and checking code, which is exactly what you have to do with an agent’s output anyway.
Project: you may use any tool; the result is what is graded. Be able to explain every line you submit.

title: Organisation
text:
Workload
One credit corresponds to 26 hours of work, so five credits are roughly two hours of lectures, two hours of lab and about four hours of your own preparation per week, plus the preparation for the exam (directive on credits).

title: Lectures
text: Open the slides, press F for full screen and ? for help. Download HTML saves a single file that works offline. To get a PDF, press E in the presentation (or add ?print-pdf to its address), then print with Ctrl+P and choose Save as PDF.

title: Lectures
text:
Lectures 2026/27


Lecture 1

Introduction, optimization, how we code now
What machine learning is; supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. Distances, 1-NN, k-NN, k-means, UPGMA. Optimization: convexity, closed-form vs. iterative solutions. Why we compute by hand and validate what an agent writes.
Tomáš Vičar

Slides Download HTML




Lecture 2

Performance evaluation, metrics, preprocessing
The supervised pipeline; train / validation / test. Confusion-matrix metrics, ROC and precision–recall, R². Class imbalance, cross-validation, scaling, missing values, outliers, and where information leaks.
Tomáš Vičar

not published yet




Lecture 3

Feature extraction, selection and dimensionality reduction
Curse of dimensionality. Filter methods (correlation, entropy, mutual information, mRMR), wrappers (forward selection, backward elimination), embedded methods. PCA, LDA, t-SNE and UMAP, feature expansion.
Tomáš Vičar

not published yet




Lecture 4 · new

Vibecoding — how coding agents work
What a coding agent is: context, tools, the agent loop. What the models can and cannot do. Specifying a task, reviewing a diff, tests as the contract, version control as the safety net. Telling correct code from plausible-looking code.
in preparation

not published yet




Lecture 5

Linear models and kernels
Linear regression and linear classification as one equation. OLS, LAD, ridge and lasso; polynomial regression. The kernel trick, primal vs. dual ridge regression. LDA, MSE classifier, logistic regression, perceptron, SVM with hard and soft margin, kernel SVM.
Tomáš Vičar

not published yet




Lecture 6

Decision trees and ensembles
Bias–variance trade-off and learning curves. CART for classification and regression: impurity, greedy splitting, stopping. Bagging, random forest and out-of-bag samples. AdaBoost step by step.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 7

Artificial neural networks
Perceptron and the artificial neuron; activation functions. Gradient for one neuron, matrix notation, the general network. Mini-batch gradient descent, Adam, saddle points. Loss functions. L1/L2 regularization, dropout, batch normalization.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 8

Convolutional networks 1 — basics
Shallow vs. deep networks and the price of depth. From fully connected to convolutional: local connections, shared weights, counting parameters. Convolutional layer, activation, pooling, dropout, batch norm; a typical CNN layer by layer.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 9

Convolutional networks 2 — special blocks
Skip connections and residual blocks. 1 × 1 convolution, bottlenecks, autoencoders. Dilated convolution and the receptive field. Up-sampling and transposed convolution. Channel and spatial attention, CBAM.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 10

Other networks — architectures and applications
Regression and classification heads, encoders. Image-to-image networks, segmentation (U-Net, nnU-Net), object detection (Faster R-CNN). Recurrent networks and LSTM. Transfer learning, pre-trained networks, augmentation.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 11

Transformers
Tokenization, embeddings, positional encoding. Self-attention in three steps: queries, keys, values; multi-head attention and its cost. Encoder, decoder, output head. Vision transformer. Pre-trained transformer models.
Jiří Chmelík

not published yet




Lecture 12 · new

Generative models and wrap-up
Proposal: diffusion models (forward and reverse process, denoising as the training objective), a short look at how large language models are trained (pre-training, fine-tuning, RLHF), and a summary of the course.
in preparation

title: Exercise 1 — Introduction, libraries, nearest neighbour
text:
What you will learn

What the four libraries of this course are for: NumPy (arrays), Matplotlib (plots), pandas (tables), scikit-learn (models).
How a real dataset is created — by measuring, writing down and cleaning up, not by downloading.
How a nearest-neighbour classifier decides: on paper, in a spreadsheet, and in NumPy — and that all three give the same numbers.
Why we write the code ourselves in the first labs, with the AI assistance switched off.

title: Exercise 1 — Introduction, libraries, nearest neighbour
text:
Before the lab

Recall from the first lecture how the Euclidean distance between two points is computed, and the 1-NN rule — find the closest training sample, predict its class.
If Python is new to you, watch the crash course below before the lab; we will not teach the language itself.
In Colab, switch off the AI features: Tools → Settings → AI Assistance, uncheck everything.

title: Exercise 1 — Introduction, libraries, nearest neighbour
text:
Tasks
A quick tour of NumPy, Matplotlib, pandas and scikit-learn comes first, with two small exercises to try. Then:

Measure your leaves — measure the height and the width of three leaves and enter them into the shared spreadsheet; this is the dataset used today and in the next lab. Look at the table before trusting it and clean up what the class mistyped.
Nearest neighbour by hand — six known leaves, one new leaf: compute the six distances on paper, first from the height alone, then from the height and the width; then the same six with one formula in a spreadsheet.
The same six leaves in NumPy — write euk_dist, loop over the six leaves, use np.argmin, and check that the numbers match the blackboard.
The whole dataset — repeat it with all the measured leaves and classify two new ones.

At the end, a first look at classes and methods — the preview of next week’s lab.

title: Exercise 1 — Introduction, libraries, nearest neighbour
text:
Data

Shared spreadsheet of the leaves — the dataset of this course, measured by you. Columns: Leaf height (cm), Leaf width (cm), Tree type (maple, cherry or walnut). It starts with three example rows, one per tree type; every student adds three more.
leaves_small.csv — the seven leaves of the by-hand task (download); the column Role says which six are the training set and which one is the new leaf.
leaf_measurement.png, leaf_measurement_height.png — how a leaf is measured: the height alone, and the height and the width as the sides of the smallest box containing the blade; in centimetres with one decimal place.

title: Exercises
text: Every lab has an assignment page (what you will learn, the tasks, the small example to compute by hand, data) and, for labs 1–4, 6–9 and 11, a notebook in Google Colab (opens from the assignment page; save a copy to your Drive before editing). Labs 5 and 10 happen in a terminal and an editor and come with a starter project instead; lab 12 is the project consultation.

title: Exercises
text:
Labs 2026/27


Exercise 1

Introduction, libraries, nearest neighbour
NumPy, Matplotlib, pandas and scikit-learn in an hour. Measure leaves, compute the nearest-neighbour decision by hand, then in NumPy.

Assignment Colab




Exercise 2

k-NN as an object, metrics, splitting, standardization
From NN to k-NN, the scikit-learn estimator interface, metrics from a confusion matrix by hand and in NumPy, hold-out split, standardization, and a broken pipeline to diagnose.

not published yet




Exercise 3

Feature selection
Tables in pandas. Correlation, entropy and mutual information by hand on eight rows, then in NumPy and checked against scipy. PCA from the covariance matrix. Forward selection from scratch and in scikit-learn, backward elimination.

not published yet




Exercise 4

Linear, ridge and kernel regression
Least squares on three points by hand. Polynomial features and why degree 15 goes wrong. Ridge with λ traced in a table before the plot; primal vs. dual; the kernel trick, kernel ridge and kernel PCA; lasso vs. ridge.

not published yet




Exercise 5 · new

Coding agents and Git
How software is written now. Installing a coding agent, Git as the safety net from here on: commits, diffs, going back when the agent breaks something. A starter project you extend with an agent — and a trap in it that only reading the diff will catch.

not published yet




Exercise 6

SVM, decision trees, random forest
SVM primal and dual, the effect of C and of the kernel. One CART split by hand with Gini and entropy, then trees, bagging and random forest in scikit-learn. Pixel-wise segmentation of aerial images. Grid vs. Bayesian search, and a first task handed to an agent.

not published yet




Exercise 7

Neural network from scratch
One learning step of a single neuron by hand, the lecture’s own numbers. A neuron and then a two-layer network in NumPy with backpropagation written out in matrix form and checked with finite differences. Activations and the learning rate.

not published yet




Exercise 8

PyTorch
Tensors and what autograd actually does; last week’s NumPy network rebuilt in PyTorch and checked against your own backpropagation. Optimizers and their state, batches, nn.Module. One 3 × 3 convolution by hand, then Dataset, DataLoader and a CNN on photos of leaves.

not published yet




Exercise 9

Deep-learning showcase with an agent
Seven tasks, one encoder: image and signal classification, segmentation, image-to-image and signal-to-signal regression. Softmax and cross-entropy by hand, one reference task (ECG noise type) worked through, then you pick a task, hand the specification to an agent and validate what comes back.

not published yet




Exercise 10 · new

Practical application on MetaCentrum
Why a notebook stops being enough once a run takes hours. A training project as scripts with arguments, checkpoints and logs, run first locally and then as a GPU job on MetaCentrum: account, job script, scratch, results. Extended with an agent and committed to Git.

not published yet




Exercise 11

Transformers
Scaled dot-product attention for three tokens by hand. Tokenization, positional encoding and a small language model trained on WikiText-2, then last year’s checkpoint generating text. An image as a sequence of patches, a pre-trained vision transformer and its fine-tuning; a transformer on ECG as an optional extra.

not published yet




Exercise 12 · new

Project
Consultation and presentation of your own project: what is fixed (one metric, a hidden test set, a repository with history, a five-minute talk), what is still to be decided, and the checklist before hand-in.

not published yet
